text: He would be revered in the East and the West alike — the rejuvenator of Hinduism in the land of his birth, and abroad, the preacher of her eternal truths. But first, he had to be born. And even his birth was a prayer, answered.

At 6:33, a few minutes before sunrise, on Monday, the twelfth of January, 1863, a son was born to the Datta family of Calcutta. It was Makarasamkranti — the day when special worship is offered to the Ganga. And so his very first breath was drawn into air already trembling with the prayers, the worship, the sacred music of thousands of Hindu men and women.

His mother, Bhuvaneswari Devi, had not merely longed for a son. Like the pious mothers of this land before her, she had taken vows. She fasted. She prayed — that she might be blessed with a son who would do honour to the family. She asked a kinsman in Kashi to offer special worship to Vireswara Siva — for Siva, the great god of renunciation, reigned over her thoughts.
And one night, she dreamed — the supreme Deity Himself roused from His meditation and agreed to be born as her son. When she woke, her heart was flooded with joy.
She received the child as a boon from Vireswara Siva, and named him Vireswara. The family gave him another name — Narendranath Datta. Narendra, for short. And, in love, simply — Naren.

The Dattas of Calcutta were known across the city — for their wealth, their philanthropy, their scholarship, and their fierce, independent spirit. And renunciation ran in their blood. His grandfather, Durgacharan, had renounced the world in search of God. Looking upon the infant, many whispered that the old renouncer had returned — reborn in this child.
We like to believe greatness is forged. But some souls seem to arrive already turned toward the Light — a vrata fulfilled, a prayer that took on a face and a name.

He came as a boon. But a boon still has to be shaped — the way a sculptor shapes stone. Two very different hands would shape this one: a worldly father, who gave him reason and a wide, clear mind, and a devout mother, steeped in the epics, who gave him truth and faith.
